text: You have an array that was sorted in ascending order, then rotated somewhere between one and n times. All values are unique. Return the minimum element, in log n time.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — after rotating, the array is two runs that each go up, with one drop between them. Like four, five, six, seven, zero, one, two: it climbs to seven, falls off a cliff to zero, then climbs again. The minimum is the bottom of that cliff. Now here's the part I want to pin down. You said rotated between one and n times. Rotating n times puts it back exactly where it started. So a fully sorted array like eleven, thirteen, fifteen, seventeen is a legal input, with no cliff at all. Is that right?
That's right. That case is in scope.

Good — I'll design around that one, because I think it's where most attempts break. Let me run through the example. For four, five, six, seven, zero, one, two, the answer is zero at index four. For eleven, thirteen, fifteen, seventeen, the answer is eleven at index zero — the very first element. So my method has to land on index zero without a special case, or the code gets ugly fast. One more thing I'll lean on: the values are unique. I'll come back to why that matters.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to scan and take the min. Correct, but that's linear, and the problem asks for log n. This problem reminds me of binary search on a predicate rather than on a sorted array. The array as a whole is not sorted, so I can't compare against a target and go left or right. But binary search never really needed sorted — it needs one constant-time question that tells me which half to keep. Here that question is: am I standing left of the cliff, or right of it? To answer it I need a fixed reference point to compare against, and picking that reference is the whole problem. There are two obvious candidates: the left end and the right end. And they are not equally good.

Here's the plan. One: anchor on nums of r. The minimum is always at or left of it — nothing sits to its right — but it's right of nums of l only if the array is actually rotated. Two: if nums of m is bigger than nums of r, the cliff sits between them and m is out, so l equals m plus one. Three: otherwise m shares r's run and might be the minimum, so r equals m. One thing worth flagging: that asymmetry is deliberate — I only skip m when I can prove it's out. Un-rotated, I just shrink left to index zero, for free. The trade-off: this rests on unique values. m is always left of r, so they never compare equal. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. Compare mid with right, skip past mid when it's bigger, otherwise pull right down to mid, and return where the two meet. One thing worth flagging: it's while left is less than right, not less than or equal. This search converges — the answer is the meeting point. With less than or equal, once left equals right, mid equals right too, the test is always false, and right equals mid changes nothing. That's an infinite loop, not a wrong answer, and zero, one is enough to trigger it. Same trap on the other side: write left equals mid instead of mid plus one, and with two slots left, nothing moves.

Let's dry-run the code with an example: four, five, six, seven, zero, one, two — expected zero. Round one carries the idea: nums of three is seven, nums of six is two. In one rising run, seven would be the smaller — it isn't, so the drop is between them, and indices zero through three go in one step. Two more rounds pull right down to index four: zero. That matches. Corner cases: a single element, the loop never runs. Eleven, thirteen, fifteen, seventeen returns eleven. Three, four, five, one, two returns one. Five thousand negatives, unrotated, returns minus five thousand. Since the shape depends only on n and the rotation, I checked all fifty-five shapes up to length ten: zero mismatches — while comparing against nums of left fails thirty-six.

The time complexity is log n — every round drops at least half the range. The space complexity is constant, three integers. In the worst case, n is five thousand: across every rotation it takes thirteen rounds, exactly the ceiling of log two of five thousand. No overflow concerns — I only compare values. Oh, one more thing — the uniqueness guarantee is doing more work than it looks. With duplicates, nums of m can equal nums of r, and then I can't tell which side the cliff is on: two, two, two, one, two and two, one, two, two, two look identical from m and r, but the minimum is on different sides. The fix is a third branch that does right minus minus — safe, but it sheds one slot, so the worst case degrades to linear. This problem is log n because of that constraint.

Good. Three things stood out. You spotted that rotated n times means an un-rotated array is legal, and designed around that case first instead of patching it later — that's why you picked the right anchor. You explained the asymmetry between the branches in terms of what you can prove — that one side rules mid out and the other doesn't. And you tied the complexity back to the uniqueness constraint with a concrete pair of arrays that look identical from the probe. Most people treat all values are unique as decoration.
